The SRF1001 is a vertical radial tape feeder engineered for smart EMS PCB assembly. Taped electrolytic capacitors, Y-capacitors, square capacitors, terminals, springs and bent resistors ride the two motor-driven feeding wheels, advance at one second per action cycle, and present themselves to the mounter head at a repeatable ±0.2 mm position. The movable cutting module trims leads to 3 – 6 mm; shaping molds and a 90° bend are options per material spacing. The 8-core aviation plug carries the IO handshake. Base S model, reliable, proven from a large install base.

01 — Why it matters

Radial parts are where an insertion line still runs on hands

Electrolytics, Y-capacitors, square capacitors, terminals, springs and bent resistors ship upright on paper tape — packaging that protects short radial leads but defeats reel-to-reel feeding. Without a dedicated radial feeder, an operator hand-stuffs them one by one: slow, tangled in bulk trays, and the most common source of polarity and spacing errors on high-mix boards. The SRF1001 turns that bench into a machine step that runs at the mounter's beat.

01

Hand insertion is the hidden bottleneck

Every radial part placed by hand costs seconds the mounter could spend placing. Multiply by boards per shift and the 'small' upright parts decide your real output — and nobody logs it because the mounter was never the constraint.

02

Bulk radial parts tangle and mis-orient

Loose electrolytics and springs in a tray tangle their leads; a person can invert polarity or miss the spacing. The SRF1001 presents one taped part at a time at a known pitch and attitude — the head either takes the right part or the fibre sensor alarms.

03

Odd-form parts starve the mounter

Without a vertical tape path, every odd-form part number means another manual lane and another stop. One SRF1001 carries the radial family — capacitors, terminals, springs, bent resistors — so lanes are swapped, not the line stopped.

02 — The method

From taped reel to pick point in six repeatable moves

Radial tape feeding is older than SMT, but the engineering is in the details: how the upright part is held, how the lead is trimmed, and how the spacing is set when the head arrives. The SRF1001 sequences it into six steps, all documented in the product document and the V03 catalogue.

01

Load the taped reel

The vertical tape drops over the two feeding wheels; the sprocket holes index on the 12.7 mm or 15 mm pitch. The leader runs forward past the front-end optical fibre head so the very first part is counted before the cycle starts.

02

Lock onto the mounter bank

The feeder seats on the machine bank with its datum and clamps in place; the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug carries 24 V and the IO handshake in one motion. No shims, no re-tramming.

03

Set the spacing

Positioning is mechanical: dividing plates define the Y-direction between parts, the limit-block position defines X. The shaping mold is matched to the material spacing so every part stands in the same attitude.

04

Feed and cut

The stepper motor — 42-type or 86-type, up to 600 rpm under PLC control — turns the two feeding wheels one pitch per cycle. The movable cutting module trims the leads to 3 – 6 mm, adjustable to the requirement.

05

The head picks

The mounter head descends and takes the upright component at ±0.2 mm. Because the pitch is set by sprocket and plate, not by vision, the pick position stays the same on cycle one and cycle five hundred thousand.

06

Return the tape

The empty carrier is transmitted and rotated back through the feeding wheel — the tape leaves the bank where it entered. A tail cut-off is optional for lines that want the leader severed.

Step sequence and mechanism details are quoted from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03 (SRF1001 page).

Built around the published document — maintainability as a design goal

Two feeding wheels, one stepper

The motor drives two feeding wheels against the tape sprocket holes — the pitch is set by mechanics, not by friction. A 42-type or 86-type stepper at up to 600 rpm under PLC control delivers the published 1 s action cycle.

Movable cutting module

The cut-lead length is adjusted to the requirement between 3 and 6 mm by moving the cutting module. The blade is made of imported material and rated at 5 million cycles — a named consumable, not a mystery part.

Shaping molds per spacing

Different shaping molds are swapped according to material spacing (optional), so the part stands in the same attitude at the pick point whether it is a Y-cap or a terminal.

90° bending option

An optional bending function folds component leads at 90° before the pick — the step that turns an upright taped part into a board-ready insertion.

Dividing-plate positioning

Y comes from dividing plates, X from the limit-block position. Two mechanical settings you can see, measure and log — no camera to calibrate, no licence fee.

8-core aviation plug, IO or standalone

The same connector carries 24 V, 0 V and the IO handshake. Run the feeder under mounter control or standalone with button operation — both modes are published in the document.

A PLC, a fibre and a plug — controls an operator actually uses

PLC control, button operation

Software control is a PLC; the published operation mode is button operation. Feed, cut and reset are physical keys — setup does not hide behind a menu tree.

Front-end optical fibre detection

A front-end optical fibre checks material presence; the feeder alarms after 3 consecutive no-material cycles. The mounter is told before it reaches for an empty pocket.

Tape return through the wheel

The used carrier is transmitted and rotated back through the feeding wheel instead of dropping into a bin — a clean bank, and an optional tail cut-off for the leader.

IO handshake with the mounter

IO communication or standalone operation through the 8-core φ16 mm plug. The feeder requests, the head takes, the cycle counter adds one — the same rhythm on Yamaha, Juki, Fuji, Panasonic, Samsung and ASM banks.

Configure the feeding around your parts

Shaping mold set

06 — Installation

Six moves from crate to first part

The published document defines the whole commissioning: mechanical mount, utilities, tape threading, plate setup, IO handshake and the cut-length tune. Plan for minutes, not hours — and have the taped reels on hand for the tuning run.

STEP 1 · Unbox and inspect

Check the body, the two feeding wheels, the movable cutting module, the optical fibre head and the 8-core aviation plug. Confirm the tape path is clean and the return wheel turns freely.

STEP 2 · Mount on the bank datum

Seat the feeder against the mounter bank datum and clamp it. The document's fixing principle is a defined datum — a loose mount is the most common cause of pitch drift at the pick.

STEP 3 · Connect air and power

0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean air to the inlet; 24 V DC through the aviation plug. The stepper draws 4 A average, 6 A peak — confirm the bank supply can carry the accel current.

STEP 4 · Thread the tape and set the plates

Drop the taped reel over the feeding wheels, run the leader past the front-end fibre, and set the dividing plates for the Y-direction and the limit blocks for X. Match the shaping mold to the material spacing.

STEP 5 · Wire the IO handshake

IO communication through the 8-core plug, or standalone button operation. Cycle the feeder in manual first: one pitch per command, one cut per cycle, alarm verified on an empty tape.

STEP 6 · Tune the cut length

Slide the cutting module until the lead trims between 3 and 6 mm to your board's requirement, then run the first-article check. Log the module position per part number — your next changeover starts from a known setting.

ARTICLE 01Radial parts are where your insertion line still runs on hands

The mounter is never the bottleneck — the bench where someone hand-stuffs electrolytics and terminals is. Here is the invisible cost chain and a five-minute audit that exposes it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

Walk the length of a busy smart EMS floor and you will find the bottleneck in the same place in almost every factory: not at the mounter, but beside it, at a small table where an operator is pressing electrolytic capacitors and terminals into boards by hand.

Taped radial parts — electrolytics, Y-capacitors, square capacitors, terminals, springs, bent resistors — arrive standing upright on paper tape, packaging that protects short leads but defeats reel-to-reel feeding. So the line absorbs them the expensive way: seconds per part, by hand, all day. Loose parts in a bulk tray make it worse: leads tangle, bodies knock over, and someone spends real minutes untangling springs before a single part is placed.

Here is the five-minute audit. Pick your three highest-volume taped radial parts. For one shift, count how many are hand-stuffed, time the pick-and-place per part with a phone stopwatch, and multiply by your monthly board volume. Then ask the second question: how many polarity reversals and spacing escapes came from that bench last quarter? The first number prices the labour; the second prices the risk.

Once the bench has a number, the alternative is simple to specify. The SRF1001 locks onto the mounter bank with an 8-core aviation plug, runs vertical tape over two motor-driven feeding wheels, and presents taped radial parts from 2 × 2 × 3 mm up to 15 × 15 × 30 mm to the head at ±0.2 mm. The movable cutting module trims leads to 3 – 6 mm; shaping molds and a 90° bend handle the attitude. One second per action cycle replaces a shift of hand-stuffing.

The compounding part: once radial parts are machine-fed, they enter your normal planning world. Cycle counts become real, changeovers get logged, and the bench's variability leaves your quality conversations. The next product introduction that ships on radial tape stops being a staffing problem — the feeder is already running.

Run the five-minute audit this week. Then send us the three part numbers, a photo of the tape and the number you found — info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 — and we will tell you, honestly, whether a radial tape feeder pays for your mix or whether hand insertion is still the right answer.

ARTICLE 02The one-second cycle: what a radial tape feeder promises your mounter

Cycle time is a promise to the head. What 1 s per action cycle actually buys you, and the two failure modes when the tape falls behind.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

There is a number printed on every radial tape feeder's specification sheet that almost nobody interrogates: the action cycle. On the SRF1001 it is one second. That single figure is either a promise to your mounter or the reason your head idles.

Think about what the mounter actually asks of the tape path. Every cycle, the head descends, takes a part, and expects the next part to be at the pick position, at the right pitch, standing in the right attitude, before it returns. If the tape path is slower than the head, the head waits. If the tape path is fast but the pitch drifts, the head mis-picks. Both failures cost the same money — they just wear different masks.

The reusable method is to compare two numbers, not one. Take your mounter's pick cycle and your board's radial component count. Multiply: that is the demand side. Now take the feeder's action cycle — 1 s per feed-and-cut for the SRF1001 — and compare: that is the supply side. If supply is faster than demand, the tape path is never the constraint. If it is slower, you need a second lane or a second feeder.

The SRF1001's 1 s figure is published in the product document alongside a ±0.2 mm feeding accuracy and a stepper drive — 42-type or 86-type, up to 600 rpm — that advances two feeding wheels one sprocket pitch at a time. The document also records a 1000-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test with no abnormalities: the two numbers that tell you the 1 s is a sustained rate, not a showroom figure.

Log the cycle time and the accuracy on your changeover card. The first time a new part family arrives, you will know from the card whether the tape path can keep up before you commit the line.

Send us your mounter's pick cycle and your radial count per board. We will tell you honestly whether one second keeps up, or whether your mix wants a second lane.

ARTICLE 0312.7 or 15 mm: the pitch decision that decides your tape inventory

Tape hole pitch sounds like a detail until purchasing orders the wrong reels. How to lock the pitch decision before the first part number arrives.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

"We ordered tape, why won't it run?" — every radial feeder supplier on earth has heard this sentence, and almost every time it comes down to one number nobody checked: the hole pitch.

The SRF1001's document is blunt about it: the feeder runs radial tape at 12.7 mm or 15 mm pitch, and the two are not interchangeable. The pitch is the distance between sprocket holes; it is what the feeding wheels index by, and it is what sets the part-to-part spacing the mounter sees. A 12.7 mm reel in a 15 mm setup mis-indexes; the head reaches into a pocket that is not where the machine was told it would be.

Here is the method: before you buy a single reel, pull your top ten radial part numbers and check the pitch printed on each supplier's tape — or measure hole-to-hole with a caliper. Group them. Most factories find two camps, and the camps are where your automation plan gets written: one pitch per feeder lane, chosen deliberately, not discovered at the bank.

For the parts inside a chosen pitch, the feeder does the rest. The vertical tape drops over the two feeding wheels, the front-end fibre counts the leader, and the dividing plates hold the Y-spacing while the limit block holds X. For a part that only ships on the other pitch, the honest answer is a second feeder configured to it — which is exactly what the five-day design service exists to quote.

Add the pitch to your part master as a required field. The first time purchasing orders 12.7 mm tape for a 15 mm lane, the system catches it before the line does — and that is the entire difference between a paper cut and a stopped shift.

Send us your ten part numbers with their pitches marked. We will tell you which lane each belongs in, and what the second lane costs — before you order a single reel.

ARTICLE 04Five million cuts: the consumable maths nobody puts on the quotation

The cutter is rated, named and replaceable. How a published blade life turns a mystery failure into a scheduled swap.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

Every quotation lists the machine. Almost no quotation lists the blade. On a radial tape feeder, that is the number that decides whether your line stops on a Tuesday night.

The SRF1001 publishes it: the cutting blade is made of imported material, the cut length adjusts between 3 and 6 mm via the movable cutting module, and the cutter service life is 5 million cycles — with the document naming the cutter a consumable. Five million cuts is not a marketing flourish; it is a maintenance budget. At one cut per action cycle, five million cycles is roughly fifty-eight days of continuous running, or a working year across two shifts and a bank of lanes.

The method is to convert the rating into a calendar. Take your daily cut count — radial parts per board times boards per day — and divide 5,000,000 by it. That quotient is your blade-swap interval, and it belongs in your maintenance plan next to the fibre-head clean. The part that fails silently is the one you never scheduled.

This is why the movable cutting module matters beyond geometry. The lead length is adjusted by moving the module, not by swapping a fixed knife, so a new part number that wants 4 mm instead of 3 mm is a slide and a re-lock — the blade's remaining life is untouched. Wear accumulates from cutting, not from tuning.

Keep spare blades on the shelf with a named part number — the documented one-day spare parts lead-time means a swap is a morning's work, not a week of waiting. Log the swap with the cycle counter, and the next five million starts clean.

Want the consumable list for your lane count? Send us your feeder count and daily volumes; we will turn the named parts into a shelf inventory with quantities, and quote the kit with the feeders.

ARTICLE 05Shape, cut, bend: three verbs that turn a bulk capacitor into a placed component

The mechanical story of the radial feeding cycle, and why the geometry matters more than the speed.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

A radial tape feeder does three mechanical verbs well, and all three are easy to take for granted until you watch them fail: it shapes the part, it cuts the lead, and — when you ask for it — it bends.

Consider what the mounter head actually sees. A taped electrolytic sits upright in a paper pocket, leads running straight down. The head wants a part that stands at a known height, at a known spacing, with leads trimmed to a known length. Between the pocket and the pick, the SRF1001's shaping molds define the attitude — swapped according to material spacing — the movable cutting module trims the leads to 3 – 6 mm, and the optional bending function folds the leads at 90° so the part seats flat instead of springing.

The product document names all three. Shaping is a mold change, matched to the spacing of your tape. Cutting is a module position, adjustable to the requirement. Bending is an option, published as a 90° fold. None of them is exotic; all of them are geometry, and geometry is what the ±0.2 mm accuracy figure is really protecting.

This is why the accuracy number matters more than it looks. The head does not pick a component; it picks a position. If the mold wears, the attitude drifts; if the blade dulls, the lead length drifts; if the limit block moves, the X-spacing drifts. The part that used to sit flat now sits at an angle — and the mounter's rejection rate tells you before your eyes do.

Keep the mold set, the cutting module gauge and a spare blade at the machine, and re-verify the first article after any change. A new blade cuts at a slightly different height, and the height changes the lead length.

Want the drawings? The product document and the V03 catalogue are linked on this page, and our engineers will check them against your board layout before you order.

ARTICLE 06Springs, Y-caps and terminals: the parts that eat mounter uptime

The awkward upright parts are the ones that stop the line. A taping-first method for the components your planner keeps forgetting.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

Ask a planner which parts stop the line and they will name the big BGA or the fine-pitch connector. Ask the operator, and they will name the springs, the Y-caps and the terminals — the small upright parts that never made it onto a reel.

Radial parts are awkward by shape: they stand up, their leads tangle, their bodies knock over in bulk trays. A spring fed loose is a spring that shorts two pads. A Y-cap inverted by hand is a field failure with a date stamp. And every minute the mounter spends waiting for someone to hand-stuff an odd-form part is a minute of six-figure-per-hour machine time idling. These parts eat uptime quietly, one placement at a time.

The method is to inventory by feeding difficulty, not by value. Take your part master and mark every radial part: taped, bulk or loose-in-tray. The taped ones are automatable today — the SRF1001 window runs from 2 × 2 × 3 mm to 15 × 15 × 30 mm with a 0.3 – 1.0 mm wire core, and covers electrolytics, Y-caps, square capacitors, terminals, springs and bent resistors. The bulk ones are a taping conversation with your supplier — a packaging decision, not an engineering project.

Once a part is taped at a known pitch, the feeder takes over the rest: two feeding wheels index the sprocket holes, the front-end fibre counts the leader and alarms after three empty cycles, the dividing plates and limit block hold the geometry, and the head picks the same part in the same attitude every second. The awkwardness was in the packaging; the packaging was the easy fix.

Watch the second-order effect over a quarter: the escapes that used to arrive from the bench stop arriving, the lane that kept feeding during the changeover keeps its schedule, and the training conversation stops being about dexterity. The parts stay the same; the line's behaviour changes.

Send us the awkward list — photos and pitches are enough. We will mark each row feed-now, feed-after-taping, or honestly 'keep it manual', with the reason.

ARTICLE 07Your odd-form feeder conversation starts with a photo, not a drawing

What a custom feeding design actually needs from you — three photos, two dimensions and one volume — and what it never needs.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

The scariest sentence in automation is 'our part is special'. The least scary version of it is a photograph.

Every feeder supplier has watched a custom project stall because a customer was asked for a drawing and does not have one — because the part is a spring, or a terminal, or a locally-sourced Y-cap with no CAD. The truth our engineering team has learned over fifteen years of custom feeding: a custom radial feeder design does not need a drawing. It needs to see the part standing up, and it needs to know how many you build.

Here is the three-photo method. Photo one: the part out of the package, next to a coin for scale — that gives us the outline inside the 2 × 2 × 3 to 15 × 15 × 30 mm window, or tells us it is outside. Photo two: the part taped, or a handful of them loose so we can see the lead span and wire core — that gives us the pitch choice, 12.7 or 15 mm, and the cutting length between 3 and 6 mm. Photo three: the board, so we can see spacing and neighbours and know whether the optional 90° bend is needed.

Then two numbers: boards per day and the loaded wage at the bench. With five inputs, the documented five-day design service returns a feeding concept — mold geometry, plate setup, cut module position, interface to your mounter — not a brochure. The SRF1001 family is explicitly published as customizable for odd-form and non-standard equipment, offering tape cutting and component bending options; the custom path is the documented path, not a favour.

Design cycles shrink when the evidence arrives early. The project that starts with three photos finishes with a first-article test on your own tape; the project that starts with a request for a drawing finishes in a shared drive.

Take the three photos today and send them to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. We will tell you within one working day whether your special part is a standard lane or a five-day design — and what each one costs.

ARTICLE 08Before you automate radial insertion, run these four numbers

A payback method with your own volumes, your own time study and your own price — plus the three savings the method deliberately leaves out.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SRF1001 product document and the Feeder Nozzle Catalog V03.

Most payback conversations about small automation are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the radial components per board — electrolytics, Y-caps, terminals, springs — the boards per day, and the seconds per hand placement you measured yourself with a stopwatch. Not the number from a brochure, your number. Line two: what does the feeder actually take over? Be honest: it automates the taped, repeatable picks, not the weird ones. Use the share your process really allows. Line three: your loaded wage and your working days. Line four: divide the quoted feeder price by the annual labour the first three lines freed. If the answer is under twelve months, this is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

The calculator on this page runs those four lines exactly, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — every money figure is typed in by you. The defaults are placeholders for the arithmetic, not claims about your factory.

Now the three savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the escapes a manual bench lets through — reversed polarity, the spring that bridged two pads, the capacitor pushed in at an angle and failed at wave solder; the mounter slot a dedicated feeder frees on a crowded bank; and the training cost of the bench itself, which is really the cost of every new hire learning your parts with their fingers.

Every factory that starts measuring radial-fed labour finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'consumables' or 'overtime'. The four lines make it visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a feeder configuration — pitch, molds, blade kit, interface — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this feeder raises

What components can the SRF1001 actually feed?
Taped radial components with an outline from 2 × 2 × 3 mm up to 15 × 15 × 30 mm and a wire core of 0.3 – 1.0 mm: electrolytic capacitors, Y-capacitors, square capacitors, terminals, springs and bent resistors. If your part ships on radial tape today, it is very likely inside the window — send a sample reel and we will confirm the presentation.
What is the difference between 12.7 mm and 15 mm tape pitch?
The pitch is the distance between sprocket holes — it defines how far the feeding wheels advance per action cycle. The SRF1001 is built for either 12.7 mm or 15 mm radial tape, and the product document is explicit: the two are not interchangeable. Choose at order time to match the tape your suppliers actually ship, or stock the feeder to your two highest-volume part families.
How fast can it feed? What throughput should I plan?
The published figure is 1 s for one action cycle — feed, cut and present — with feeding accuracy of ±0.2 mm. The tape path presents parts faster than the mounter head can take them, so throughput is set by the machine's pick cycle, not the feeder. The document also records a 1000-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test with no abnormalities.
How long does the cutter last, and what does it cost to keep?
The blade is made of imported material and the published cutter service life is 5 million cycles — the cutter is explicitly named a consumable. At one cut per second, five million cycles is roughly fifty-eight days of continuous running, so plan a scheduled blade swap per shift-hours consumed rather than an emergency call. Spare blades ship in a day.
What are the power and utility requirements?
24 V DC at 4 A average / 6 A peak, and 0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean compressed air. Power and signals arrive through the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug; air feeds the cut and bend actuators. The feed itself is motor-driven — a 42-type or 86-type stepper at up to 600 rpm under PLC control.
How does the feeder talk to the mounter?
IO communication through the aviation plug, or standalone operation with button control — both modes are published. The front-end optical fibre detects material presence and alarms after 3 consecutive no-material cycles, so the head is never sent to an empty pocket.
What do the shaping and bending options actually do?
Shaping molds are replaced according to material spacing so each part stands in the same attitude at the pick point (optional). The bending function folds leads at 90° before the pick (optional). Together they are the difference between a part that is presentable and a part that is placement-ready.
How do I get a quotation?
Send a photo of your taped components, the tape pitch (12.7 or 15 mm), the board volumes and your machine list to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a mold and plate configuration, a spare blade kit proposal and a price — usually within one working day, with a sample feeding test available before you commit.
